title: When Does Generating More Help? Disentangling Fixed-Source Synthesis from Source Expansion in Synthetic Data Scaling

paper.title: When Does Generating More Help? Disentangling Fixed-Source Synthesis from Source Expansion in Synthetic Data Scaling
paper.abstract:
Abstract Synthetic data can be scaled along two routes: Source Expansion (SE), which enlarges the source by adding seed materials or generators,
and Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS), which holds the source fixed and scales the generation budget.
Existing scaling studies typically expand the source as the data grows, conflating SE with FSS and leaving FSS underexplored.
We isolate FSS by holding the seed-question pool and teacher model fixed, varying only the per-question response budget under Rejection Sampling (RS).
We adapt the rectified scaling law to FSS, deriving it from how repeated sampling covers a fixed source.
Empirically, the derived form, fit on low budgets, predicts performance at the held-out highest budget for every evaluated teacher–student pair.
At matched total-sample budgets, SE and FSS are comparable at small budgets; at large budgets, adding seed questions outperforms spending the same budget on more responses.
Within FSS, however, neither synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds nor varying the synthesis protocol outperforms plain RS at matched budgets.
FSS is thus a bounded scaling axis and a controlled setting for comparing synthesis protocols.
We will release our code and data to facilitate further research.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Synthetic data is now standard in training large language models (LLMs) ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Mukherjee et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2025a ; Toshniwal et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2024 ) . Prior studies report that downstream performance scales predictably with synthetic datasets ( Ge et al., 2024 ; Yue et al., 2024 ; Busbridge et al., 2025 ) . Figure 1: Two routes for scaling synthetic data. S ource E xpansion ( SE ) enlarges the information sources (the seed set and generator), while F ixed- S ource S ynthesis ( FSS ) holds the source fixed and scales only the generation budget. However, synthetic data scales along two distinct routes. A synthetic dataset can grow either by enlarging the source (adding documents, seed questions, or generators), or by holding the source fixed and scaling the generation budget. We refer to these as source expansion (SE) and fixed-source synthesis (FSS), respectively (Fig. 1 ). Recent studies scale along the SE route: Yue et al. (2024) retrieve more web documents and extract a few instructions per document, and Qin et al. (2025) expand the source-document pool for math while holding per-document generation fixed. These are natural practices for building corpora, but they scale along SE, leaving FSS returns underexplored. We isolate FSS within a standard synthesis pipeline: the source is a pair ( Q , T ) (Q,T) of a seed-question pool Q Q and a teacher T T ; FSS fixes ( Q , T ) (Q,T) and scales the per-question response budget r r via rejection sampling (RS), while SE enlarges Q Q or switches T T . Within this setup, we ask three research questions: ∘ \circ RQ1. With the source ( Q , T ) (Q,T) fixed, does FSS improve student accuracy, and how does the gain scale with r r ? ∘ \circ RQ2. At matched total-sample budgets, how do SE and FSS gains compare? ∘ \circ RQ3. Within FSS, do common synthesis protocols (diversifying, selecting, or rewriting the synthetic data) improve over plain RS? For RQ1, we scale r r under RS and trace student accuracy on two domains (Mathematics, Physics). For RQ2, we run two comparisons at a fixed total-sample budget: expanding the real seed pool Q Q (SE) versus increasing r r at fixed ( Q , T ) (Q,T) (FSS); and synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds versus plain RS. For RQ3, we evaluate common synthesis protocols (alternative sampling temperatures, embedding-based selection, persona prompting, unfiltered sampling, and trace-level repair) against plain RS under the same fixed-source control. In total, synthetic-data construction consumes about 2 2 B teacher-inference tokens ( 1.6 1.6 B from DeepSeek-V3.1 rollouts), followed by over 500 500 student SFT runs (more than 2,000 2{,}000 GPU-hours of fine-tuning). Below, we summarize the key findings for each RQ. ∘ \circ FSS gains diminish with r r and leave a clear teacher–student gap at the largest budget; a fixed-source form, derived from repeated sampling and fit on low budgets, predicts performance at the held-out highest budget for every evaluated teacher–student pair. ∘ \circ At matched total-sample budgets, SE and FSS are comparable at small budgets, but expanding the real seed-question set (SE) becomes the more reliable axis as the budget grows; synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds yields no gain over plain RS. ∘ \circ Under the fixed-source control, common synthesis protocols do not consistently improve over plain RS, so protocol p p contributes little once the source ( Q , T ) (Q,T) is fixed.

sections.heading: Scaling laws for synthetic-data fine-tuning.
sections.text: Scaling laws characterize how pre-training loss varies with model size and training tokens, providing a principled basis for compute allocation ( Hestness et al., 2017 ; Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . Subsequent studies extend this view beyond pre-training tokens, covering data-constrained scaling under limited unique tokens ( Muennighoff et al., 2023 ; Lovelace et al., 2026 ) and the role of teacher strength in distillation ( Bansal et al., 2025 ) . A closer sub-line targets fine-tuning: Hernandez et al. (2021) characterize transfer from pre-training, Lin et al. (2024) propose a rectified scaling law for fine-tuning, and Qin et al. (2025) apply this rectified law to synthetic-data fine-tuning. These studies scale synthetic data by enlarging the source. In contrast, we fix the source ( Q , T ) (Q,T) and trace SFT scaling within FSS alone.

sections.heading: Synthetic Data Generation.
sections.text: A second line of work targets the synthesis protocol p p . Prompt-synthesis methods generate new prompts from the seed set ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2025a ; Yue et al., 2024 ) . Sampling-side methods alter teacher-trace generation, either by reallocating generation budget across teachers or samples ( Bansal et al., 2025 ) or through prompt-side conditioning such as persona-driven generation ( Ge et al., 2024 ) . Data curation methods act on the resulting candidates: embedding- or gradient-based selection ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Xia et al., 2024 ) retains compact, high-value subsets, while filtering controls how much teacher noise enters training, including settings that omit filtering or use negative reasoning traces as supervision ( Mukherjee et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2025b ) . Critique-and-revise methods rewrite weak or incorrect traces ( Madaan et al., 2023 ; Kapusuzoglu et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . These studies, however, evaluate protocols across heterogeneous teachers and seed corpora, entangling the effect of p p with that of ( Q , T ) (Q,T) . We therefore re-evaluate representative protocols per strand in a teacher–student setting with ( Q , T ) (Q,T) fixed, so that gains reflect p p alone.

sections.heading: 3 Source Expansion vs. Fixed-Source Synthesis
sections.text: We model a synthetic-data pipeline as a triple ( Q , T , p ) (Q,T,p) : a seed-question set Q Q , a teacher T T , and a synthesis protocol p p that turns seeds into training examples through choices of prompt template, decoding parameters, filtering, selection, or rewriting. For each seed q ∈ Q q\in Q , p p generates one or more SFT examples from ( q , T ) (q,T) ; the training set is the multiset of all such examples. We distinguish two routes for enlarging this set: ∘ \circ Source expansion (SE) alters ( Q , T ) (Q,T) by adding real seed questions from outside the pool, or switching to a stronger or additional teacher. ∘ \circ Fixed-source synthesis (FSS) fixes the source ( Q , T ) (Q,T) and varies only the protocol p p or the per-question budget r r , including protocols that synthesize new prompts from the existing seeds. The three RQs partition this triple: Sec. 5 fixes ( Q , T ) (Q,T) and sweeps the per-question budget r r (FSS); Sec. 6 matches total-sample budgets between SE (scaling | Q | |Q| ) and FSS (scaling r r ); Sec. 7 fixes ( Q , T ) (Q,T) and varies the synthesis protocol p p .

sections.heading: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.text: The setup below is shared across all three RQs; implementation details appear in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Domains.
sections.text: We study two reasoning domains from SuperGPQA ( Du et al., 2026 ) : Mathematics and Physics . Tab. 1 reports train/test sizes and per-domain teacher references.

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: The primary teacher is DeepSeek-V3.1 ( dv31 ; T DS T_{\mathrm{DS}} ), and the primary student is Qwen2-7B-Instruct ( S Q7 S_{\mathrm{Q7}} ). We use a second teacher ( Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct ; T Q72 T_{\mathrm{Q72}} ) and a second student ( Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ; S L8 S_{\mathrm{L8}} ) for the cross-pair RQ1 checks and fixed-source audit in Appendix A.6 . The heterogeneous-source check in Sec. 8 uses Qwen3-4B ( S Q3 S_{\mathrm{Q3}} ) as the student.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: Each student is fine-tuned by SFT for the same number of epochs. For cells with repeated SFT runs, we use n = 3 n{=}3 training seeds and report mean ± std \mathrm{mean}\pm\mathrm{std} .

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: The primary metric is mean ​ @ ​ 8 \mathrm{mean@8} : for each test question, we sample 8 8 student responses at temperature 0.7 0.7 and report the mean fraction correct. Averaging over 8 8 samples reduces per-question sampling noise and stabilizes the comparisons below.

sections.heading: 5 RQ1: Fixed-Source Synthesis Scaling
sections.text: This section quantifies how far FSS alone can raise student performance under a fixed source ( Q , T ) (Q,T) . We define the source-determined ceiling that bounds FSS, derive a three-parameter form for the response-budget curve P ⁡ ( r ) P(r) , and identify the budget at which the empirical curve flattens.

sections.heading: 5.1 Response-scaling form for FSS
sections.text: A common parametric form for fine-tuning data scaling is the rectified scaling law ( Lin et al., 2024 ) , L ⁡ ( D ) = B D ℓ + D β + E , L(D)\;=\;\frac{B}{D_{\ell}+D^{\beta}}+E, (1) where D D is the fine-tuning data size, L ⁡ ( D ) L(D) the validation loss, E E the irreducible error as D → ∞ D\to\infty , B > 0 B>0 an amplitude, β > 0 \beta>0 the scaling exponent, and D ℓ > 0 D_{\ell}>0 a rectification constant capturing the model’s pre-learned competence. Qin et al. (2025) apply this form to synthetic data with L ⁡ ( D ) L(D) as the test error rate. Substituting the test accuracy P = 1 − L P=1-L into Eq. 1 gives P ⁡ ( D ) = ( 1 − E ) − B D ℓ + D β , P(D)\;=\;(1-E)\;-\;\frac{B}{D_{\ell}+D^{\beta}}, (2) i.e. a fixed ceiling 1 − E 1-E minus a term that vanishes as D → ∞ D\to\infty . In the rectified-law reading, 1 − E 1-E is the asymptote of the underlying prediction task: an irreducible residual that no additional data removes, set by the task’s intrinsic noise. FSS differs in the origin of its bound. The scaling axis is no longer data but a budget spent on a fixed source: with ( Q , T ) (Q,T) held fixed and only the per-question response budget r r growing, each additional draw rephrases or diversifies the same fixed content. The relevant asymptote is therefore different. It is no longer the prediction task’s irreducible-error ceiling 1 − E 1-E , which assumes an unbounded ideal data source, but a source -determined ceiling P ∞ ​ ( Q , T ) P_{\infty}(Q,T) : the best test performance reachable while ( Q , T ) (Q,T) is held fixed. We retain the parametric family of Eq. 2 and re-derive its functional form under this fixed-source view. To derive the shape of P ⁡ ( r ) P(r) , we model the source through discrete latent features f f , following the quanta view of Michaud et al. (2023) : individually learnable units of skill or reasoning that a student either acquires or does not. Coverage is binary : a feature contributes if at least one training sample exposes it, with no partial credit. Let q ⁡ ( f ) q(f) denote its per-sample exposure probability. Under i.i.d. draws, f f remains uncovered after r r samples with probability ( 1 − q ⁡ ( f ) ) r (1-q(f))^{r} , giving P ⁡ ( r ) = P ∞ − 𝔼 f ​ [ ( 1 − q ⁡ ( f ) ) r ] P(r)=P_{\infty}-\mathbb{E}_{f}[(1-q(f))^{r}] . Our distributional assumption is that q ⁡ ( f ) q(f) follows a long-tailed (power-law) distribution over features, as predicted by the same quanta view. We then split the expectation 𝔼 f ​ [ ( 1 − q ⁡ ( f ) ) r ] \mathbb{E}_{f}[(1-q(f))^{r}] by feature frequency. Common features are covered within a few draws, with miss probability decaying exponentially in r r ; once r r is moderate, the rare -feature tail dominates the residual gap to P ∞ P_{\infty} . Under a power-law tail, this residual decays polynomially in r r , giving P ⁡ ( r ) ≈ P ∞ − A ​ r − α , P(r)\;\approx\;P_{\infty}-A\,r^{-\alpha}, (3) the offset-free ( D ℓ = 0 D_{\ell}{=}0 ) case of Eq. 2 with source-determined ceiling P ∞ P_{\infty} . Performance thus rises quickly while common features are covered, then approaches P ∞ P_{\infty} at the polynomial rate r − α r^{-\alpha} . The full derivation is deferred to Appendix A.1 .

sections.heading: 5.3 Analysis for RQ1
sections.text: Tab. 2 and Figs. 2 – 3 report the results, from which we draw two observations.

sections.heading: (i) FSS shows diminishing returns in the response budget.
sections.text: Across Mathematics, Physics, and all four teacher–student pairs, student accuracy keeps rising with r r . The budget axis is logarithmic, so a steadily climbing curve corresponds to a shrinking gain per additional response. This is consistent with the saturating form of Eq. 3 : with ( Q , T ) (Q,T) held fixed, early responses cover the common features, while later responses increasingly repeat already-covered signal and reach the rare tail only occasionally, so the marginal gain per response shrinks.

sections.heading: (ii) A stronger teacher raises the source ceiling.
sections.text: Although diminishing returns appear in all settings, the ceiling depends on the teacher. Within the scanned grid, T Q72 T_{\mathrm{Q72}} begins to flatten. On the same seed set and student, T DS T_{\mathrm{DS}} surpasses T Q72 T_{\mathrm{Q72}} and keeps rising. The stronger teacher thus lifts the source ceiling above the level the weaker teacher can reach.

sections.heading: Summary.
sections.text: RQ1 supports the fixed-source scaling hypothesis: FSS consistently improves student accuracy, but its marginal gains diminish as the response budget r r grows. Saturation sets in earlier under the weaker teacher and later under the stronger one, so the benefit of an FSS depends jointly on r r and teacher strength. sections.heading: 6 RQ2: Matched-Budget SE and FSS Gains
sections.text: This section asks two matched-budget questions. First, when we add real seed questions, how does SE compare with spending the same budget on more responses from fewer seeds? Second, when we synthesize new prompts from existing seeds, do they outperform an RS baseline?

sections.heading: Paradigm 1: add new seed questions.
sections.text: Let Q 4 Q_{4} denote the full real seed-question pool. Let Q 1 ⊂ Q 2 ⊂ Q 4 Q_{1}\subset Q_{2}\subset Q_{4} be nested random subsets holding one-quarter and one-half of its questions, respectively, so that | Q q | = q 4 ​ | Q 4 | |Q_{q}|=\tfrac{q}{4}|Q_{4}| . We sweep the RS response budget r r and compare allocations matched on the number of SFT examples. An allocation ( q , r ) (q,r) yields | Q q | ⋅ r = q 4 ​ | Q 4 | ⋅ r |Q_{q}|\cdot r=\tfrac{q}{4}|Q_{4}|\cdot r examples, so the budget depends only on the product q ⋅ r q\cdot r . A smaller question pool therefore matches the full pool only by raising r r in proportion. We index a matched-budget bucket by this product, B ≡ q ⋅ r ∈ { 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } B\equiv q\cdot r\in\{4,8,16,32\} : bucket B B collects ( q = 4 , r = B / 4 ) (q{=}4,\,r{=}B/4) , ( q = 2 , r = B / 2 ) (q{=}2,\,r{=}B/2) , and ( q = 1 , r = B ) (q{=}1,\,r{=}B) . At B = 4 B{=}4 , for instance, Q 4 Q_{4} draws one response per question while Q 1 Q_{1} draws four. As B B grows, the smaller- | Q | |Q| allocations spend more responses on fewer seeds. We therefore predict that the larger- | Q | |Q| allocation wins at larger B B , because repeated sampling from a smaller seed pool should yield diminishing returns sooner. We run this matched-budget triple on both Mathematics and Physics, so the prediction is tested cross-domain.

sections.heading: Paradigm 2: question synthesis as FSS.
sections.text: We synthesize additional prompts from the full real seed set for Mathematics and Physics using an instruction-evolution procedure ( Xu et al., 2025a ) , with our primary teacher T DS T_{\mathrm{DS}} (DeepSeek-V3.1) as the synthesis model; format and similarity filtering leave ∼ 4 × \sim\!4\times as many prompts as the seed set, on which we sweep r ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } r\in\{1,2,4,8\} under the same RS protocol. Because these prompts derive from the existing seeds rather than new source material, question synthesis stays within the fixed source. We compare against the RS baseline under two references (Fig. 5 ): the fixed- r r reference compares the synthesized-question condition at r = k r{=}k with RS on the original seeds at the same r = k r{=}k , so the synthesized side contributes more SFT examples; the matched-budget reference compares it with RS at r = 4 ​ k r{=}4k , holding the total SFT examples equal so the comparison isolates how the synthesized prompts spend the fixed-source budget. Figure 6: RQ3 audit on Mathematics. Each panel overlays one audited protocol’s r r -sweep (blue, averaged over n = 3 n{=}3 training seeds) on the shared RS baseline (dashed line). Bands show the train-seed standard deviation. Shading between the protocol and RS curves is blue where the protocol exceeds the baseline and red where it falls below. The bottom-right annotation reports the shift in the intrinsic metric from the RS reference to the audited pool (Jaccard distance for diversity protocols, wrong-response % for filter ablations, rewrite share for trace-rewrite variants). Each protocol shifts its targeted intrinsic metric, yet none yields a stable gain at its best r r .

sections.heading: 6.2 Analysis for RQ2
sections.text: Figs. 4 and 5 address one question: under a fixed budget, where should the next training example go? We compare three uses of that example: a new real seed question, an additional response to an existing seed, and a question synthesized from existing seeds. We have the following two findings.

sections.heading: (i) The next example is better spent on a new real seed than on more responses to existing seeds.
sections.text: On Physics, q = 4 q{=}4 is the best allocation at every budget; on Mathematics, q = 4 q{=}4 matches q = 1 q{=}1 at low budget and overtakes it at high budget (Fig. 4 ). This is consistent with the fixed-source account: extra responses to a few seeds exhaust their limited source signal, whereas new seed questions add coverage that resampling existing seeds cannot supply.

sections.heading: (ii) When no new real seed is available, the next example is better spent on another real response than on a synthesized question.
sections.text: Under the fixed- r r reference, synthesized questions beat the same- r r RS baseline (Fig. 5 , solid bars). Under the matched-budget reference the comparison reverses: once the total SFT-example count is equalized, more responses from the original seeds beat synthesized questions (Fig. 5 , hatched bars). This result is specific to a fixed synthesis budget and to questions directly conditioned on the existing seeds. A larger synthesis budget, or a different downstream task setting, may still make synthesized questions worthwhile.

sections.heading: Summary.
sections.text: RQ2 asks how to allocate a fixed budget across data sources. The matched-budget comparison isolates the cause: the apparent payoff of prompt synthesis is a budget effect, not a synthesis effect. Once the example count is held equal, prompts synthesized from existing seeds underperform plain re-sampling of the original seeds.

sections.heading: 7 RQ3: Synthesis Protocols at Fixed Budget
sections.text: Under fixed ( Q , T ) (Q,T) , we ask whether any synthesis protocol improves over the RS reference. Fig. 6 overlays each audited protocol’s r r -sweep on the shared RS baseline.

sections.heading: 7.1 Experiments for RQ3
sections.text: The audited methods are listed below. All audited protocols and their implementation details are provided in Appendix A . ∘ \circ Temperature variants : replace the RS sampling temperature ( 1.2 1.2 ) with 0.6 0.6 or 0.001 0.001 . ∘ \circ Embedding-based selection : from the RS pool, pick r r responses per question to maximize pairwise embedding distance, following the diversity criterion of DEITA ( Liu et al., 2024 ) ; the r = 1 r{=}1 and r = 32 r{=}32 endpoints match RS by construction. ∘ \circ Persona prompting : prepend a persona sampled from PersonaHub ( Ge et al., 2024 ) as a system message before each teacher generation. ∘ \circ Judge-free / filter ablation : drop the correctness judge to admit wrong teacher traces, connecting to work that uses negative reasoning as supervision ( Mukherjee et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2025b ) ; a prompt-aligned variant pins the prompt set to the RS subset, isolating response filtering from question coverage. ∘ \circ Trace-level repair : rewrite wrong teacher responses into a wrong → \to check → \to fix trace, adapting iterative-refinement and critique-then-revise recipes ( Madaan et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Kapusuzoglu et al., 2025 ) ; a second variant keeps only the revised correct solution.

sections.heading: Intrinsic metrics.
sections.text: For each protocol, we pair the transfer outcome with an intrinsic scalar of the audited SFT pool that should shift when the intervention takes effect. Response diversity , the mean pairwise token-set Jaccard distance across the retained responses per question, tracks the temperature, persona, and embedding-selection variants (reported at r = 8 r{=}8 for the latter). Correctness noise , the final-answer mismatch rate in the pool, tracks the no-judge variants. Rewrite share , the fraction of wrong → \to check → \to fix traces in the pool, tracks the trace-repair variants.

sections.heading: Audited variants do not surpass RS.
sections.text: Fig. 6 shows that each audited protocol moves its targeted intrinsic metric, yet transfer tracks the RS baseline across the method × r \times r grid. Response diversity, correctness noise, and correction-signal share each shift under their variants, but the Physics replication yields the same outcome (Tab. 5 ), and averaging each method’s gap to RS over the full r ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } r\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\} sweep yields no consistent positive advantage (Appendix A.4 ).

sections.heading: Summary.
sections.text: This decoupling between intrinsic shifts and transfer holds within the fixed-source regime tested here; under a different source pool, or with larger teacher or question budgets, the same generation protocols may still contribute on top of RS. Cross-pair replication with a weaker teacher and a different student again shows no gain over RS (Appendix A.6 ). Figure 7: Matched-budget allocation on mixed STEM domains. The ‘more questions ( r = 1 r{=}1 )’ series scales the seed-question pool; the other two hold the question set at 8 8 w/ 16 16 w and raise r r . This question-coverage allocation stays strictly above both at every matched budget, and the gap widens with budget.

sections.heading: 8 Robustness on a Heterogeneous Source
sections.text: The main RQ1 and RQ2 experiments use single-domain slices. We relax this single-domain restriction and adopt a heterogeneous source: the STEM set of Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v2 ( Basant et al., 2025 ) , which mixes STEM domains instead of isolating one domain. We stress-test both findings on a single matched-budget grid, reading it two ways. Each fixed-pool series traces an FSS response-scaling path (RQ1). The comparison across pool sizes at a fixed total budget is the matched-budget SE-vs-FSS test (RQ2). Here the seeds added at larger | Q | |Q| are drawn from a mixture of STEM domains rather than a single one. We use T DS T_{\mathrm{DS}} (DeepSeek-V3.1) as the teacher and S Q3 S_{\mathrm{Q3}} ( Qwen3-4B ) as the student, chosen to keep training cost tractable on this larger heterogeneous pool, and defer source-pool construction, the validation split, and training settings to Appendix A.7 . Fig. 7 addresses both questions on a single grid. For RQ1, the two fixed-pool series ( 8 8 w and 16 16 w) climb only marginally on the log 2 \log_{2} budget axis. This reproduces, on a larger and more heterogeneous source, the diminishing-returns pattern RQ1 established on per-domain slices. For RQ2, the r = 1 r{=}1 path, which raises real-question coverage, climbs steeply instead. Its advantage over both fixed-pool series widens as the budget grows, and at the matched 32 32 w total-example budget it lies above both. On a heterogeneous source, both results hold: the FSS bound persists, and at a fixed total budget, more real seed questions outperform drawing more responses from a smaller seed pool, even when those added seeds span multiple STEM domains.

sections.heading: 9 Discussion
sections.text: The central distinction is whether a scaling intervention alters the source support or only reallocates budget within it. Our three questions probe this contrast through different interventions. Scaling the per-question response budget (Sec. 5 ) draws more traces from the fixed source, with diminishing returns on a logarithmic budget axis; synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds (Sec. 6 ) enlarges the question pool but, at a matched total budget, does not outperform simply sampling more responses; substituting an alternative synthesis protocol (Sec. 7 ) changes how traces are drawn from the same source but does not improve over the RS reference. Only source expansion escapes this pattern, along both axes of ( Q , T ) (Q,T) : adding real seed questions yields a matched-budget advantage on per-domain slices (Sec. 6 ) and on the heterogeneous source (Sec. 8 ), and a stronger teacher raises student accuracy at the same sample budget (Sec. 5 ). Under the coverage model (Appendix A.1 ), source expansion raises the reachable ceiling, whereas within-source interventions redistribute samples beneath it. This view explains why FSS scales but is bounded, and why matched-budget comparisons should separate source expansion from within-source synthesis before attributing gains to synthetic-data scaling.

sections.heading: 10 Conclusion
sections.text: We separate synthetic-data scaling into Source Expansion (SE) and Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS), then isolate FSS by holding ( Q , T ) (Q,T) fixed. Across our experiments, FSS follows a bounded response-scaling curve captured by the fixed-source form, while matched-budget gains come from expanding the source rather than reshuffling synthesis within it. The fixed source therefore provides a controlled setting for evaluating synthesis protocols.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Prior synthetic-data scaling work focuses primarily on reasoning. Although we cover broader STEM tasks, extending to further domains is left to future work. Our experiments are computationally expensive. When the teacher is large (for example, DeepSeek-V3.1), generation cost is high, and doubling the sampling budget exceeds our compute envelope. Larger sampling budgets are a natural next step. Finally, we fix a teacher–student setting across experiments for fair comparison. However, synthetic data spans more tasks, and a broader exploration of synthesis methods and deployment scenarios is left to subsequent work.

sections.heading: A.1 Derivation of the FSS response-scaling form
sections.text: We derive Eq. 3 from a binary feature-coverage model under four modelling assumptions: binary coverage, linear additivity, (near-)i.i.d. exposure, and a heavy-tailed feature-frequency distribution. The heavy-tail assumption is independently motivated by the long-tailed skill-usage frequencies documented by Michaud et al. (2023) , who tie precisely such a power-law frequency structure to neural scaling. The empirical fits in Sec. 5 test the resulting functional form in aggregate rather than verify each assumption pointwise.

sections.heading: When the heavy-tail step fails.
sections.text: The coverage model above implies monotonicity and discrete concavity for any distribution of q ⁡ ( f ) q(f) , but the power-law rate requires mass near q = 0 q=0 . If g g instead concentrates away from zero, for example in a roughly homogeneous regime q ⁡ ( f ) ≈ q q(f)\approx q , then 𝔼 f ​ [ ( 1 − q ⁡ ( f ) ) r ] ≈ ( 1 − q ) r ≈ e − q ​ r \mathbb{E}_{f}[(1-q(f))^{r}]\approx(1-q)^{r}\approx e^{-qr} , yielding exponential rather than polynomial saturation. If g g consists of well-separated bands, the gap becomes a sum of exponentials with distinct rates. These alternatives would still be monotone and concave, but would not obey the three-parameter form of Eq. 3 ; the empirical fits in Sec. 5 therefore test the pure-power tail approximation rather than the coverage model as a whole.

sections.heading: Relation to the rectified scaling law.
sections.text: The derived form is, algebraically, the offset-free member of the family of Eq. 1 : writing the accuracy curve as an error rate ( L = 1 − P L=1-P ), P ⁡ ( r ) = ( 1 − E ) − A ​ r − α P(r)=(1-E)-A\,r^{-\alpha} matches Eq. 3 with P ∞ = 1 − E P_{\infty}=1-E and the same power, i.e. Eq. 2 at D ℓ = 0 D_{\ell}{=}0 with D D replaced by r r . The agreement is one of functional form only, and the two differ where it matters. The fitted floor E E of Eq. 1 is a model-capacity and task quantity, whereas P ∞ P_{\infty} here is, under (i)–(iii), the contribution mass of features the fixed source can ever expose to the student under a held-constant student and training protocol; variation in P ∞ P_{\infty} across fixed-source sweeps is thus interpreted as variation in the source’s reachable mass given that fixed student, rather than as a capacity limit revealed by increasing data quantity. The absence of D ℓ D_{\ell} is likewise not a fitted simplification but a consequence of conditioning on a fixed source: source expansion, which converts features with q ⁡ ( f ) = 0 q(f)=0 to q ⁡ ( f ) > 0 q(f)>0 (the mechanism behind the SE/FSS separation in Sec. 6 ), moves the process outside this offset-free fixed-source derivation and would re-introduce the additional flexibility associated with D ℓ D_{\ell} in Eq. 1 . The external law thus fixes the functional family; the fixed-source mechanism selects its offset-free member and re-interprets the ceiling.

Disentangling Fixed-Source Synthesis from Source Expansion in Synthetic Data Scaling Xu Guo Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory Affiliation: Shanghai Innovation Institute Affiliation: Fudan University Jian Tong Affiliation: Shanghai AI Laboratory Zhihui Lu Qipeng Guo Email: {tongjian, guoqipeng}@pjlab.org.cnguox24@m.fudan.edu.cn lzh@fudan.edu.cn † Corresponding authors Affiliation: Shanghai Innovation Institute Abstract Synthetic data can be scaled along two routes: Source Expansion (SE), which enlarges the source by adding seed materials or generators, and Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS), which holds the source fixed and scales the generation budget. Existing scaling studies typically expand the source as the data grows, conflating SE with FSS and leaving FSS underexplored. We isolate FSS by holding the seed-question pool and teacher model fixed, varying only the per-question response budget under Rejection Sampling (RS). We adapt the rectified scaling law to FSS, deriving it from how repeated sampling covers a fixed source. Empirically, the derived form, fit on low budgets, predicts performance at the held-out highest budget for every evaluated teacher–student pair. At matched total-sample budgets, SE and FSS are comparable at small budgets; at large budgets, adding seed questions outperforms spending the same budget on more responses. Within FSS, however, neither synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds nor varying the synthesis protocol outperforms plain RS at matched budgets. FSS is thus a bounded scaling axis and a controlled setting for comparing synthesis protocols. We will release our code and data to facilitate further research. 1 Introduction Synthetic data is now standard in training large language models (LLMs) ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Mukherjee et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2025a ; Toshniwal et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2024 ) . Prior studies report that downstream performance scales predictably with synthetic datasets ( Ge et al., 2024 ; Yue et al., 2024 ; Busbridge et al., 2025 ) . Figure 1: Two routes for scaling synthetic data. S ource E xpansion ( SE ) enlarges the information sources (the seed set and generator), while F ixed- S ource S ynthesis ( FSS ) holds the source fixed and scales only the generation budget. However, synthetic data scales along two distinct routes. A synthetic dataset can grow either by enlarging the source (adding documents, seed questions, or generators), or by holding the source fixed and scaling the generation budget. We refer to these as source expansion (SE) and fixed-source synthesis (FSS), respectively (Fig. 1 ). Recent studies scale along the SE route: Yue et al. (2024) retrieve more web documents and extract a few instructions per document, and Qin et al. (2025) expand the source-document pool for math while holding per-document generation fixed. These are natural practices for building corpora, but they scale along SE, leaving FSS returns underexplored. We isolate FSS within a standard synthesis pipeline: the source is a pair ( Q , T ) (Q,T) of a seed-question pool Q Q and a teacher T T ; FSS fixes ( Q , T ) (Q,T) and scales the per-question response budget r r via rejection sampling (RS), while SE enlarges Q Q or switches T T . Within this setup, we ask three research questions: ∘ \circ RQ1. With the source ( Q , T ) (Q,T) fixed, does FSS improve student accuracy, and how does the gain scale with r r ? ∘ \circ RQ2. At matched total-sample budgets, how do SE and FSS gains compare? ∘ \circ RQ3. Within FSS, do common synthesis protocols (diversifying, selecting, or rewriting the synthetic data) improve over plain RS? For RQ1, we scale r r under RS and trace student accuracy on two domains (Mathematics, Physics). For RQ2, we run two comparisons at a fixed total-sample budget: expanding the real seed pool Q Q (SE) versus increasing r r at fixed ( Q , T ) (Q,T) (FSS); and synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds versus plain RS. For RQ3, we evaluate common synthesis protocols (alternative sampling temperatures, embedding-based selection, persona prompting, unfiltered sampling, and trace-level repair) against plain RS under the same fixed-source control. In total, synthetic-data construction consumes about 2 2 B teacher-inference tokens ( 1.6 1.6 B from DeepSeek-V3.1 rollouts), followed by over 500 500 student SFT runs (more than 2,000 2{,}000 GPU-hours of fine-tuning). Below, we summarize the key findings for each RQ. ∘ \circ FSS gains diminish with r r and leave a clear teacher–student gap at the largest budget; a fixed-source form, derived from repeated sampling and fit on low budgets, predicts performance at the held-out highest budget for every evaluated teacher–student pair. ∘ \circ At matched total-sample budgets, SE and FSS are comparable at small budgets, but expanding the real seed-question set (SE) becomes the more reliable axis as the budget grows; synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds yields no gain over plain RS. ∘ \circ Under the fixed-source control, common synthesis protocols do not consistently improve over plain RS, so protocol p p contributes little once the source ( Q , T ) (Q,T) is fixed. 2 Related Work Scaling laws for synthetic-data fine-tuning. Scaling laws characterize how pre-training loss varies with model size and training tokens, providing a principled basis for compute allocation ( Hestness et al., 2017 ; Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . Subsequent studies extend this view beyond pre-training tokens, covering data-constrained scaling under limited unique tokens ( Muennighoff et al., 2023 ; Lovelace et al., 2026 ) and the role of teacher strength in distillation ( Bansal et al., 2025 ) . A closer sub-line targets fine-tuning: Hernandez et al. (2021) characterize transfer from pre-training, Lin et al. (2024) propose a rectified scaling law for fine-tuning, and Qin et al. (2025) apply this rectified law to synthetic-data fine-tuning. These studies scale synthetic data by enlarging the source. In contrast, we fix the source ( Q , T ) (Q,T) and trace SFT scaling within FSS alone. Synthetic Data Generation. A second line of work targets the synthesis protocol p p . Prompt-synthesis methods generate new prompts from the seed set ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2025a ; Yue et al., 2024 ) . Sampling-side methods alter teacher-trace generation, either by reallocating generation budget across teachers or samples ( Bansal et al., 2025 ) or through prompt-side conditioning such as persona-driven generation ( Ge et al., 2024 ) . Data curation methods act on the resulting candidates: embedding- or gradient-based selection ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Xia et al., 2024 ) retains compact, high-value subsets, while filtering controls how much teacher noise enters training, including settings that omit filtering or use negative reasoning traces as supervision ( Mukherjee et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2025b ) . Critique-and-revise methods rewrite weak or incorrect traces ( Madaan et al., 2023 ; Kapusuzoglu et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . These studies, however, evaluate protocols across heterogeneous teachers and seed corpora, entangling the effect of p p with that of ( Q , T ) (Q,T) . We therefore re-evaluate representative protocols per strand in a teacher–student setting with ( Q , T ) (Q,T) fixed, so that gains reflect p p alone. 3 Source Expansion vs. Fixed-Source Synthesis We model a synthetic-data pipeline as a triple ( Q , T , p ) (Q,T,p) : a seed-question set Q Q , a teacher T T , and a synthesis protocol p p that turns seeds into training examples through choices of prompt template, decoding parameters, filtering, selection, or rewriting. For each seed q ∈ Q q\in Q , p p generates one or more SFT examples from ( q , T ) (q,T) ; the training set is the multiset of all such examples. We distinguish two routes for enlarging this set: ∘ \circ Source expansion (SE) alters ( Q , T ) (Q,T) by adding real seed questions from outside the pool, or switching to a stronger or additional teacher. ∘ \circ Fixed-source synthesis (FSS) fixes the source ( Q , T ) (Q,T) and varies only the protocol p p or the per-question budget r r , including protocols that synthesize new prompts from the existing seeds. The three RQs partition this triple: Sec. 5 fixes ( Q , T ) (Q,T) and sweeps the per-question budget r r (FSS); Sec. 6 matches total-sample budgets between SE (scaling | Q | |Q| ) and FSS (scaling r r ); Sec. 7 fixes ( Q , T ) (Q,T) and varies the synthesis protocol p p . 4 Experimental Setup The setup below is shared across all three RQs; implementation details appear in Appendix A . We define the source-determined ceiling that bounds FSS, derive a three-parameter form for the response-budget curve P ⁡ ( r ) P(r) , and identify the budget at which the empirical curve flattens. 5.1 Response-scaling form for FSS A common parametric form for fine-tuning data scaling is the rectified scaling law ( Lin et al., 2024 ) , L ⁡ ( D ) = B D ℓ + D β + E , L(D)\;=\;\frac{B}{D_{\ell}+D^{\beta}}+E, (1) where D D is the fine-tuning data size, L ⁡ ( D ) L(D) the validation loss, E E the irreducible error as D → ∞ D\to\infty , B > 0 B>0 an amplitude, β > 0 \beta>0 the scaling exponent, and D ℓ > 0 D_{\ell}>0 a rectification constant capturing the model’s pre-learned competence. Qin et al. (2025) apply this form to synthetic data with L ⁡ ( D ) L(D) as the test error rate. Substituting the test accuracy P = 1 − L P=1-L into Eq. 1 gives P ⁡ ( D ) = ( 1 − E ) − B D ℓ + D β , P(D)\;=\;(1-E)\;-\;\frac{B}{D_{\ell}+D^{\beta}}, (2) i.e. a fixed ceiling 1 − E 1-E minus a term that vanishes as D → ∞ D\to\infty . In the rectified-law reading, 1 − E 1-E is the asymptote of the underlying prediction task: an irreducible residual that no additional data removes, set by the task’s intrinsic noise. FSS differs in the origin of its bound. The scaling axis is no longer data but a budget spent on a fixed source: with ( Q , T ) (Q,T) held fixed and only the per-question response budget r r growing, each additional draw rephrases or diversifies the same fixed content. The relevant asymptote is therefore different. It is no longer the prediction task’s irreducible-error ceiling 1 − E 1-E , which assumes an unbounded ideal data source, but a source -determined ceiling P ∞ ​ ( Q , T ) P_{\infty}(Q,T) : the best test performance reachable while ( Q , T ) (Q,T) is held fixed. We retain the parametric family of Eq. 2 and re-derive its functional form under this fixed-source view. To derive the shape of P ⁡ ( r ) P(r) , we model the source through discrete latent features f f , following the quanta view of Michaud et al. (2023) : individually learnable units of skill or reasoning that a student either acquires or does not. Coverage is binary : a feature contributes if at least one training sample exposes it, with no partial credit. Let q ⁡ ( f ) q(f) denote its per-sample exposure probability. Under i.i.d. draws, f f remains uncovered after r r samples with probability ( 1 − q ⁡ ( f ) ) r (1-q(f))^{r} , giving P ⁡ ( r ) = P ∞ − 𝔼 f ​ [ ( 1 − q ⁡ ( f ) ) r ] P(r)=P_{\infty}-\mathbb{E}_{f}[(1-q(f))^{r}] . Our distributional assumption is that q ⁡ ( f ) q(f) follows a long-tailed (power-law) distribution over features, as predicted by the same quanta view. We then split the expectation 𝔼 f ​ [ ( 1 − q ⁡ ( f ) ) r ] \mathbb{E}_{f}[(1-q(f))^{r}] by feature frequency. Common features are covered within a few draws, with miss probability decaying exponentially in r r ; once r r is moderate, the rare -feature tail dominates the residual gap to P ∞ P_{\infty} . Under a power-law tail, this residual decays polynomially in r r , giving P ⁡ ( r ) ≈ P ∞ − A ​ r − α , P(r)\;\approx\;P_{\infty}-A\,r^{-\alpha}, (3) the offset-free ( D ℓ = 0 D_{\ell}{=}0 ) case of Eq. 2 with source-determined ceiling P ∞ P_{\infty} . Performance thus rises quickly while common features are covered, then approaches P ∞ P_{\infty} at the polynomial rate r − α r^{-\alpha} . (i) FSS shows diminishing returns in the response budget. Across Mathematics, Physics, and all four teacher–student pairs, student accuracy keeps rising with r r . Our three questions probe this contrast through different interventions. Scaling the per-question response budget (Sec. 5 ) draws more traces from the fixed source, with diminishing returns on a logarithmic budget axis; synthesizing additional questions from the existing seeds (Sec. 6 ) enlarges the question pool but, at a matched total budget, does not outperform simply sampling more responses; substituting an alternative synthesis protocol (Sec. 7 ) changes how traces are drawn from the same source but does not improve over the RS reference. Only source expansion escapes this pattern, along both axes of ( Q , T ) (Q,T) : adding real seed questions yields a matched-budget advantage on per-domain slices (Sec. 6 ) and on the heterogeneous source (Sec. 8 ), and a stronger teacher raises student accuracy at the same sample budget (Sec. 5 ). Under the coverage model (Appendix A.1 ), source expansion raises the reachable ceiling, whereas within-source interventions redistribute samples beneath it. This view explains why FSS scales but is bounded, and why matched-budget comparisons should separate source expansion from within-source synthesis before attributing gains to synthetic-data scaling. 10 Conclusion We separate synthetic-data scaling into Source Expansion (SE) and Fixed-Source Synthesis (FSS), then isolate FSS by holding ( Q , T ) (Q,T) fixed. Across our experiments, FSS follows a bounded response-scaling curve captured by the fixed-source form, while matched-budget gains come from expanding the source rather than reshuffling synthesis within it. The fixed source therefore provides a controlled setting for evaluating synthesis protocols. Limitations Prior synthetic-data scaling work focuses primarily on reasoning. Although we cover broader STEM tasks, extending to further domains is left to future work. Our experiments are computationally expensive. When the teacher is large (for example, DeepSeek-V3.1), generation cost is high, and doubling the sampling budget exceeds our compute envelope. Larger sampling budgets are a natural next step. Finally, we fix a teacher–student setting across experiments for fair comparison. However, synthetic data spans more tasks, and a broader exploration of synthesis methods and deployment scenarios is left to subsequent work.
